activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A referee or umpire is the person who makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Rowan played on a basketball team. He wore a red shirt with the number five. His sister came to watch every game. She sat on the long bench by the court.

Bounce, bounce, bounce went the ball. Rowan ran. He passed. He shot. The ball hit the rim. Then Rowan ran fast with it. A whistle blew. Loud and sharp.

"Who is that man?" Rowan asked. "Why did he blow the whistle?"

"He is the referee," said Coach. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Rowan had run too far with the ball. That was not the rule. So the other team got the ball now. Rowan puffed out his cheeks. Then he nodded.

Next practice, Rowan counted his steps. One, two, then he stopped. Bounce, bounce, bounce. He passed to his friend Ben. Ben shot. The ball went in. The referee gave a thumbs up.

After the game, Rowan waved to his sister. "The referee watched me," he said. "I followed the rules." He yawned all the way to the car, and he fell fast asleep before they got home.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: The hairdresser puts a cape around your shoulders to keep cut hair off your clothes.
story:
Kinsley held her toy pig tight. "Pig needs a haircut too," she said.

Mom laughed. "You are the one getting a haircut today. We must not be late."

At the mall, the hairdresser smiled. She put a big cape around Kinsley's shoulders. The cape was red and shiny.

"I am a superhero!" said Kinsley. "Zoom, zoom!"

The hairdresser began to cut. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off the cape. Plop, plop, plop.

Kinsley watched one hair. It fell on her arm. She blew it away. "Bye bye, hair!" she said.

Then more hairs fell. One, two, three. They all slid off the cape. None went on her dress.

"Pig is safe too," said Kinsley. She tucked pig under the cape. Pig peeked out.

"Superhero pig," said the hairdresser.

Snip, snip, snip. Then the cape came off. Kinsley's dress was clean. No hairs on it at all.

"Look, Mom! Nothing on me!"

Mom spun her around. Kinsley hugged pig and zoomed out the door.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: A recipe tells a cook what to use and what to do, one step at a time.
story:
Penelope wants to make pancakes for her family. She asks her dad to help. Dad says, "We need the recipe." The recipe is a card that hangs on the wall.

Penelope stirs the flour and the milk. She cracks two eggs into the bowl. Dad cooks the pancakes in the hot pan. But the pancakes come out flat. They look like little flat clouds. Penelope says, "Oh no, they are so flat!"

Dad reads the recipe card again. "Look," he says. "We skipped a step. The recipe says to add the baking powder." Penelope adds it and stirs. Dad cooks the new pancakes. They come out big and puffy. The family eats them all. Penelope's little brother, a boy with smelly socks, laughs and asks for more. Penelope says, "The recipe told us what to do, one step at a time."

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: On your birthday, you turn one year older.
story:
Hunter ran into the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a table with a cake. His grandma waved at him.

A girl named Mia ran up to him. "I was three yesterday," she said. "Today I am four. It is my birthday."

Hunter looked at the cake. It had four candles. His dad lit them with a long match. Dad was careful with the flame. "Now you are four," Dad said. "You were three yesterday. On your birthday, you turn one year older."

Hunter touched the soft feather on his party hat. He thought about that. Yesterday he was three. Today the candles showed four.

"Blow them out," said Grandma.

Hunter took a big breath. He blew. The little flames went out. Smoke curled up like a feather.

Everyone clapped. Mia clapped the loudest. "Happy birthday, Hunter," she said. "You are four, just like me."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing, and a sprout does not come up right away.
story:
Alexander dug a small hole in the backyard. His dad helped him plant three little seeds. "Now what?" Alexander asked. "Seeds need water," said Dad. Alexander filled his watering can. He poured the water over the dirt. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He looked at the dirt. There was only dirt. No sprout. No green. He touched the soil with one finger. "Still wet," he said. He watered the seeds again. A bird watched him from the swing. Alexander swung slowly and waited.

The next day, only dirt again. Alexander watered the seeds one more time. Then he saw something new. A tiny green sprout was peeking out. "It came up!" Alexander shouted. He stuck out his tongue at the bird. "See? Water helped it grow!" The sprout stood there, small and green, in the morning sun.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Apples, bread and carrots are all foods.
story:
Iris wanted to sort her toys. She put the robot in one pile. She put the white bear next to it. Then she found a carrot on the rug. It had rolled off the table. She put the carrot with the toys.

At lunch, Mom set out plates. "Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Mom. Iris looked at her toys. The carrot did not belong there! She ran back and wiped the rug where the carrot had been. Then she carried the carrot to the food bowl.

The carrot went crunch when she bit it. It tasted sweet. Mom put apple slices beside her. The bread was soft and warm. Iris fed the robot a pretend apple. The robot said nothing. Iris laughed and patted his white round head. "You can't eat," she said. "You're a toy."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
story:
Alexis ran to the big drum at the park. He hit it with his hands. Boom! Boom! Boom! His whole body felt excited. "I am a giant!" he shouted. His voice was big like thunder.

A girl named Mia came close. Then the drum went boom again. Mia covered her ears with both hands. She ran behind the bench. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked scared.

Alexis stopped drumming. He felt sad that Mia was sad. He thought hard. Then he patted the drum very softly. Tap. Tap. Mia peeked out. Her hands came down. She smiled a happy smile. "I like it quiet," she said. "I like it loud," said Alexis. They looked at each other. Same drum. Different feelings.

"I know!" said Alexis. "We can count the taps." He tapped softly. Mia counted. "One, two, three." They sat close together on the cozy grass. Then Mia took a paper plate from her bag. She held it up like a tiny drum. Tap, tap, went the quiet plate. Alexis tapped his big drum. Soft, then loud, then soft. They made a drum song all their own, one giant and one small, playing side by side in the sun.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Norah sat at the paint table. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. "Where is the orange?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Beth, smiled. "Let's look at the cups."

The cups held red, blue, yellow, and green paint. Norah sniffed one cup. "This red one smells stinky," she said, and she giggled. Miss Beth laughed too. "That is okay. Paint can smell like that." Sam, who sat close by, pushed his brush toward her. "Put red in the yellow," he said. "Watch what happens."

Norah dipped her brush in red. She stirred it into the yellow cup. Swirl, swirl, swirl. The paint turned orange! "It changed!" she cried. She painted her pumpkin orange. It looked round and bright. Miss Beth hung it up to dry. "I want to pay you a sticker," Miss Beth said, and she stuck a shiny gold star on Norah's hand. Norah held it up high. "My pumpkin is orange," she said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
story:
Theodore ran into art class. "Today we hunt for shapes!" said Miss Amy. She held up a red card. It had four sides and four square corners. "This is a rectangle," she said. "Can you find one?" Theodore looked and looked. He saw a round clock. "No, that's a circle," he said. He saw a block with equal sides. "No, that's a square." Then he saw the big door. He ran to it and put his finger on a corner. "One, two, three, four!" He counted four corners. "The door is a rectangle!"

"I found one! I found one!" Theodore shouted. Miss Amy clapped. The other kids came to see. Theo pointed up. "The door has four sides too. Just like my red card." Everyone counted the corners together.

Then Theodore got to work. He drew a tiny door on his paper. He painted a rectangle door with blue paint from the bucket. "My rectangle can open!" he said. He cut it out and taped it on. Miss Amy spelled his name at the top. Theodore held up his picture and smiled. "Look at my door!"

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We hear with our ears.
story:
William sat on the clean grass in the backyard. He wanted to name his five senses. He touched a smooth seed with his fingers. "Fingers are for touching," he said. He sniffed a red flower with his nose. "Nose is for smelling," he said.

Then a bee went buzz, buzz. William turned his head. "Which body part hears that?" he asked himself. He covered his ears with his hands. The buzz got very small. He took his hands away. The buzz came back. "Ears! We hear with our ears," he said.

William sat very still. His ears heard a bird sing. His ears heard leaves go swish. His ears heard water drip from the hose. He smiled and cupped his hands behind his ears. A dog barked next door. William laughed and said, "Hello, dog!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil point can break if you press down very hard.
story:
Myles sat at the big art table. He had a paper and a pencil. He wanted to draw a furry dog. The teacher, Miss Ana, hung a picture of a dog on the wall.

Myles began to draw. He pressed down very, very hard. He wanted the dog to be dark. He pressed even harder. Then something went snap! The pencil point broke off. It began to fall to the floor. Myles watched the little point land by his shoe.

"Oh no," said Myles. "My pencil broke." Miss Ana came over. She gave him a new pencil. "What will you try now?" she asked. Myles looked at the new pencil. He held it softly.

This time he pressed gently. The line was light and soft. He made one small mark, then another. The furry dog began to appear. Myles drew two ears and a happy tail. He smiled and looked at his paper.

"Look at my dog!" he said.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
story:
Jake was eating breakfast with his fork. His tummy felt funny. Today he had to get a shot.

"Will the shot hurt?" Jake asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then it is done."

Mom gave him a cute teddy bear to bring. "His name is Boo," Jake said. He put Boo in his bag. They got in the car.

At the doctor's office, Jake sat on the big chair. Boo sat on his lap. Jake's hands squeezed Boo tight. His legs wanted to wiggle. The nurse came in with the tray.

Grandpa held Jake's hand. "Smell the flower," Grandpa said. He held up one finger like a flower. "Breathe in slow. One, two, three."

Jake sniffed the flower finger. One, two, three. Then he blew out slow, like blowing out a candle. His shoulders came down. His hands let Boo go soft.

"Again," said Grandpa.

One, two, three in. Slow breath out. Jake did it two more times. His tummy felt less jumpy.

"Can Boo do it too?" Jake asked.

"Yes," said Grandpa. "Help him."

Jake lifted Boo to his nose. One, two, three in. Slow breath out.

"Ready?" said the nurse.

Jake kept breathing. In slow, out slow. He felt a tiny pinch, and then it was done.

"All done," said the nurse. She gave Boo a bandage too.

At home, Mom made lunch. Jake used his fork to feed himself bite by bite. He fed Boo a pretend bite. One, two, three, yum.

"Boo did it," Jake said. "And I did it too."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Yesterday, Athena and Mommy went to the store. The bread was all gone. "Come back tomorrow," said the man.

Today is tomorrow now. Athena holds Mommy's hand in the store. She wants the pink cake with sprinkles. She sees it high on the shelf.

"Can we get the pink cake?" she asks. "Soon," says Mommy. "We get bread first, and cake later."

Athena does not like soon. She wants the cake now. She sits down on the floor. Her foot taps, taps, taps.

A boy waits by the window too. "The bus comes soon," his dad says. "Soon means in a little while," the dad says. Athena listens. A little while. Not a long while.

Athena counts to ten. Then she counts to ten again. The boy points. "The bus is here!" The bus came after just a little while.

Athena jumps up. She helps Mommy put bread in the cart. She puts in apples too. Then they walk to the cake shelf.

Mommy lifts the pink cake down. "You waited," Mommy says. "You showed me how." Athena smiles big. In the bus ride home, the cake sits on her lap. She looks out the window. "Tomorrow we can eat more," she says.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: The small pictures on a tablet screen are called icons, and tapping one opens an app.
story:
Lennon went to the library with Dad. She saw the big red tablets on the small table. She wanted to draw a cloud on one.

Dad pushed the round button. The screen lit up. "Now tap the little pictures," Dad said. "They are called icons." Lennon tapped a cat icon. A cat game came up. That was not drawing.

She looked again. She saw a little paintbrush icon. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. There were colors everywhere. Lennon drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a noisy blue bird next to it.

A boy came to the table. He wanted a turn. Lennon was done anyway. She pressed the button and the screen went dark. Dad put the tablet back on the shelf. The boy waved at her. "Thank you," he said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: After using the toilet, we flush and then wash our hands.
story:
Rowan sat at the dinner table. He ate his pasta with a spoon. The pasta was warm and squishy in his mouth. He patted his full tummy.

Then Rowan needed the toilet. He ran down the hall. He used the toilet. He pulled up his pants. He ran back to the table.

"Did you flush?" asked Mom.

Rowan stopped. Oops. He had forgotten. He ran back. He pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. Then he washed his hands with soap. The bubbles smelled like flowers. He dried his hands on the towel.

Rowan ran back again. "I flushed and washed my hands!" he said.

"Good job," said Mom. "Now finish your pasta. Then it will be bath time, and after that, your cozy sock and sleepy time."

Rowan looked at his clean hands. They smelled like flowers too. He smiled and ate one more bite.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: A pretend tea party can use empty cups with no real tea in them.
story:
Ayla went to the park with her grandma. Ayla brought Bear and Bunny. She wanted to have tea with them. But she had no tea.

Ayla sat on the grass. She found two little cups by the sandbox. Someone had left them there. The cups were empty. No water. No tea. Nothing.

"Grandma, no tea!" said Ayla. Grandma smiled. "You can pour pretend tea," she said. Ayla tipped the empty cup over Bear. Nothing came out. But Ayla made a poury sound. "Glug, glug!"

Bear got a pretend drink. Bunny got a pretend drink too. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" said Ayla. Bunny tipped over. "Oops, Bunny!" said Ayla. "Don't break your cup." She set Bunny up straight again.

Then Grandma pretended to sip. "Mmm," she said. "Yummy pretend tea." Ayla giggled. She poured more pretend tea. "One more cup, Grandma?" she asked. Grandma held out her hands and said, "Yes, please."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many celebrations have special foods made just for that day.
story:
Felix wanted to taste the honey cake. Grandma was baking it in the oven. "Not yet," said Grandma. "This cake is for tonight."

"But why?" asked Felix. "Cake is cake!"

Grandma laughed. "This cake is for the holiday. We make it just for this day."

Felix watched Grandma take the pan out. She used big mitts. The cake looked brown and warm. Felix sniffed the air. "It smells yummy now," he said.

"We wait for Papa and Nia," said Grandma. "Then we eat it together."

Felix waited. He looked at the cake. He looked at the clock. The clock was very slow.

At last Papa came home. Nia came too. Felix helped Grandma lift the cake onto a big plate. Nia put out plates and forks.

"Now?" asked Felix.

"Now," said Grandma.

Everyone sat at the table. Felix took a big bite. "Happy holiday!" he said, with crumbs on his chin.

Papa patted his sleepy head. "One more little piece," said Papa, "and then bed."

"Two pieces," said Felix.

Grandma laughed. "Okay, one big one."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: A hairdresser uses a comb to keep hair neat while cutting it.
story:
Iris went to the salon with Grandma. Her hair was long and it went into her eyes. "Time for your first haircut," said Grandma. Iris felt her tummy jump. She wanted to see, but she also wanted to hide.

A hairdresser named Jo came over. Jo held a comb and a small card with hair pictures on it. Iris picked the card. "This one," she said. Jo smiled.

Then Jo combed Iris's hair. Comb, comb, comb. Then one little snip. Iris kicked her feet under the cape. "Why do you comb so much?" she asked. "Watch and see," said Jo. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. The comb made the hair lie flat and neat. Then the cut was tidy too. Iris counted, "Three combs, one snip!" Jo laughed.

At the end, Iris looked in the mirror. No hair in her eyes. She was happy. "Grandma, the comb helps the hair stay neat!" said Iris. Grandma took a photo, and Jo gave her the little card to keep.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn.
story:
Levi stood at the running track. The sun made the red track feel warm under his shoes. Coach Ana had a big bag of beanbags and a hoop on the ground.

"Watch me," she said. She threw a beanbag. It landed in the hoop. Levi clapped. Then Levi threw one. It went in too. He grabbed another beanbag. Then another. Then another.

"Levi," said a kid named Mia. "I want a turn too." Coach Ana held up her hand. "Taking turns means one throws, and then the next kid throws." Levi looked at the beanbags in his arms. He counted them in his head. Then he passed them down the line, one by one. Mia threw hers. It missed. She tried again and it landed in the hoop with a soft plop.

Levi picked up the big ball next. He held out both hands. "Ready?" asked Mia. She rolled it to him. He caught it and hugged it tight. It smelled like rubber and grass.

"My turn again?" Levi asked. Coach Ana smiled and pointed at the kid at the end of the line. Levi marched the ball over to him. "Here you go," Levi said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Charles sat on the big couch. It was Sunday morning. Everyone came to watch the big game. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too.

A man ran onto the field. He wore a black and white striped shirt. "Who is that?" Charles asked. "He is not playing ball." Uncle Ben laughed. "That is the referee," he said. "The referee watches the game. He makes sure the players follow the rules."

The referee blew his whistle. One player had pushed another player. The whistle made everyone stop. Then the game started again.

"The whistle is loud," Charles said. "It is not scary," Grandma said. "It keeps the game fair."

Later, Charles swept his toy cars off the floor with his hands. "I am the referee," he said. He held up his toy whistle. "Beep! Everybody follow the rules!"

Dad laughed and pulled Charles onto his lap.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A power cut can make all the houses on a street go dark at once.
story:
The lights went out. The big TV went dark too. Leo stood very still in the dark living room. "Mama!" he called.

Mama came with a candle. The flame tickled the air with its little light. "A power cut," said Mama. "The lights are off. We will use candles."

Leo looked at the window. He pressed his nose to the cold glass. All the houses on the street were dark! Next door was dark. The yellow house was dark. Every house on the street was dark at once. "Mama, look! All dark!"

Mama came to look. "Yes," she said. "All the houses went dark together." Leo clapped his hands. The dark street felt like a big night team, everyone the same.

Mama lit one more candle. Then another. The room got brighter and brighter. Leo got his blanket. He and Mama sat by the candles. "Now we tell a story," said Mama. "Story time can start early tonight." Leo snuggled close. The candle flames wiggled on the wall. Outside, the street stayed dark, all of it, all at once.

Then the lights popped back on. Leo blinked. "Again!" he shouted, pointing at the candles. Mama laughed and blew them out, one by one.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Freshly fallen snow is white.
story:
Gabriel was at Grandpa's house. Outside, snow was falling. It covered the grass. It covered the big green tree. Now the tree was white. "Snow is white," said Grandpa.

Gabriel wanted to draw the snow. Grandpa gave him white paper. Gabriel drew with his red crayon. He drew with his yellow crayon. He drew with his green crayon. Then he looked for a white crayon. He had no white one. The white paper had no snow on it at all. Gabriel frowned. "My snow will not show up," he said.

Grandpa looked in the drawer. He pulled out blue paper. "Try this," he said. Gabriel drew on the blue paper. He drew white snow with a cotton ball. The snow showed up! It was white on the blue. Gabriel laughed.

He drew a white hill. He drew a white snowman with a red hat. Grandma came in with warm soup. "Is it salty?" asked Gabriel. He took a little sip. Then he held up his drawing. "Look! Snow!" Grandma gave him a wave. Gabriel waved back.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby.
story:
Luca sat in the car with Dad. They were going to get the new baby. "I want to hold her," said Luca. "First we wash our hands," said Dad. "Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby."

At home, the baby was in a soft blanket. Luca ran in fast. "Hold baby now!" he said. Mom stopped him. "Hands first," she said. Luca looked at his hands. They had dirt on them.

Luca went to the sink. Dad turned on the water. Luca washed one hand, then the other. He counted, "One, two, three bubbles!" Then his hands were clean.

Mom put the baby in Luca's arms. The baby made a tiny sound. Luca gasped. She grabbed his finger! "She likes me," said Luca. Dad said, "Yes. Big brother, clean hands, warm baby." Luca smiled and held on.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
story:
Asher stood at the school gate. He held his new backpack in his hands. It was very heavy. He could not lift it onto his back.

A girl named Maya stood by him. She wore rain boots. The gate was wet and slippery from the morning rain. "My backpack goes on my back," Maya said. She turned around to show him. It sat on her back like a little nest.

Asher tried again. He pulled and pulled. The backpack slid off. It fell with a thump. Asher sat down on the step and opened it. Inside were his toy truck, three rocks, and a small plastic cow from the farm set.

Asher took out the rocks. He took out the truck. He kept the cow. Now the backpack was light. He slipped his arms through the straps. It sat on his back, just like Maya's.

Asher waved to his mom by the fence. "Look! It's on my back!" he called. The cow peeked out of the top pocket, as if she wanted to wave too.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Charlie was building a tall tower. Her blocks went up and up. Her brother Sam made a tower too. Sam's tower was very tall.

Charlie wanted to see it close. She stepped back. She bumped right into Sam's tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sam's face went funny. His lip wobbled. "My tower," he said.

Mummy knelt down by Charlie. "Say sorry," she said softly. "Sorry shows Sam you know you hurt him."

"Sorry, Sam," said Charlie.

Then Charlie picked up a block. She put it at the bottom. Sam put one on top. They took turns. One for Sam, one for Charlie.

Soon a new tower stood tall. It was even taller than before.

"Better tower?" asked Charlie.

"Yes," said Sam. "Best tower."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: A person's name is written with a capital letter at the start.
story:
Zoey sat at the little red table. Miss Pam held up a big card. "This is Z," she said. "Z says zzz, like a bee."

Zoey tapped her name tag. Z for Zoey. Zzz for Zoey. "Z is my letter!" she said.

Then Ben wrote his name on his paper. He wrote it small: ben. Miss Pam shook her head kindly. "Look," she said. She pointed at Zoey's name tag. "Your name starts with a big capital letter."

Zoey looked at her tag. Yes! Big Z, then little o, little e, little y. A name starts with a big capital letter.

Ben rubbed out his small b. He made a big tall B. "Ben!" he read. His face went bright.

Zoey picked up her pencil. She wrote her whole name. Big Z first. "I did it!" she said. Miss Pam clapped.

At play time, Zoey wrote Ben's name too. Big B, then e, then n. She wrote it on his paper next to his drawing of a fish that could swim fast in the blue water.

"My name looks beautiful," said Ben.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: If you lose something in a busy place, you tell your grown-up instead of going to search by yourself.
story:
Willow wanted her little bunny. She looked in her toy box. Bunny was not there.

The kitchen was full of people. Grandma was cooking. Aunt Jo was carrying a big bag. Willow wanted to run and look under the table all by herself. But she stopped. She went to Mommy first.

"Mommy, bunny is gone," said Willow. "Will you help me look?"

"Yes, let's look together," said Mommy.

They looked under the table. They saw a yucky old crumb. They looked by the sink. Willow heard a little scratch, scratch sound. It was the puppy! Bunny was under the puppy's blanket.

"Found her!" said Willow. She hugged bunny tight.

Mommy smiled. "I am glad you told me first."

Willow held bunny's soft ear. "Bunny was hiding," she whispered.

Then she gave Mommy a big, warm hug too.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Writing your name on your things helps them find their way back to you.
story:
Blake marched down the school hallway with her mama. The hallway was huge and full of noisy shoes. Blake held a lunchbox with a dog on it. "Will I find my cubby?" she asked. Her mama said, "Yes, I will walk with you."

At lunch, Blake set her lunchbox on the big table. A boy sat down next to her. He had a lunchbox with a dog on it too. It looked just like hers. He picked up her lunchbox by mistake. He started to walk away with it.

"Wait," Blake said. "That one is mine." The teacher came over. She opened the lid. "Look, it says Blake," she said. "The name on the lid shows whose it is." The boy found his own lunchbox. His name was Sam. Blake shared her crackers with Sam. Then they both ate lunch together.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pockets in a coat can hold small things like mittens.
story:
Wren was in the kitchen with Mom. Snow was falling outside the window. "We can play in the snow after lunch," said Mom.

Wren ate her lunch. Then she got her red coat. She pushed her arm in one sleeve. She pushed her arm in the other sleeve. She pulled the zipper up. It went halfway. She tried again. Up it went, all the way to the top! "I did it myself," said Wren.

She put on her mittens and ran outside. She made a snowball. Then she lost one mitten in the snow. "Where did it go?" she said. She looked and looked. She found it, but then she dropped it again. Wren looked at her coat. She saw the pocket. She tucked both mittens into the pocket. "Pockets can hold my mittens," she said. She zipped her coat again and made a pretty snowball, big and round.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: An eraser can rub out a pencil mark you want to fix.
story:
Victor sat at the little table in the school library. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. He held the pencil in his fist. The pencil slipped. He made a wobbly line.

Ms. Rosa sat down next to him. "Hold it like this," she said. She showed him her fingers. Victor tried. He held the pencil with his fingers, not his fist. He made a big letter V. Then a wobbly, messy letter i.

Victor felt sad. He wanted his name to look nice. "It went wrong," he said.

"Try the pink end," said Ms. Rosa. "That is called an eraser." Victor rubbed the pink end on the wobbly letter. He looked at the paper. The wobbly mark was gone!

Victor rubbed again. "It went away!" he said. He made a new letter i, straight and small. Then a c, a t, an o, and an r. He wrote Victor, all by himself.

"I did it!" said Victor. "I did it!" He showed Ms. Rosa the paper. She clapped her hands.

"What fun," said Victor. He turned the paper over. He wanted to write his name again.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day.
story:
Charles went to the art studio with his mama. He carried his box of crayons. He wanted to draw a big sun. At the studio, he opened his box. He pulled out a red crayon. But the crayon felt funny. It was soft and bendy. It bent like a noodle in his hand.

Charles had left his crayons in the car. The car sat in the sun all morning. The sun made the car hot. The hot car made the crayons melt. Now they were soft and squishy. Charles tried to draw with the bendy crayon. It just made a fat, shiny smudge. He tried again. It made another smudge.

"I want to draw my sun," said Charles. Miss Ada, the studio teacher, came over. She looked at the soft crayons. "Let's try something new," she said. She helped Charles break the bendy crayons into little bits. Charles put the bits on his paper. He made a circle of red bits and orange bits.

Then Miss Ada used the studio's warm press. Charles stood back and watched from a safe spot. He waited. He waited a little more. Then Miss Ada opened the press. The crayon bits had melted flat. They mix together into one big red-orange circle. The circle was shiny and smooth.

"It's my sun!" said Charles. "It's big and shiny!" He held up his paper. The sun was red and orange and bright. Charles drew rays with a yellow crayon that had stayed hard. His sun hung on the studio wall. "I left crayons in a hot car," Charles told his mama, "and they got soft like this!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In ice hockey, players use sticks to hit a flat disc called a puck.
story:
Addison sat in a big booth at the restaurant. A giant screen glowed on the wall. People were skating on ice. Addison's dad said, "It's a hockey game."

Addison watched the players. She looked and looked. "Where is the ball?" she asked. Her cousin Ben laughed kindly. "No ball," he said. "They hit a puck. It's flat like a little plate."

Addison watched closer. Each player held a long stick. A player swung his stick. He hit the puck. The puck slid fast across the smooth ice. "He hit it!" Addison said. "The stick made it go!"

A player on the blue team hit the puck hard. It slid all the way in. The net moved. Everyone in the restaurant cheered. Addison clapped her hands. Her mom filled her cup with juice.

"I like the puck," Addison said. She took a big bite of her bread. On the screen, a root player swung his stick again. "Hit it!" Addison called. "Hit the puck!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A triangle has three sides and three corners.
story:
Ibrahim sat at the art table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to make a house. But his house looked wobbly. "Where is the roof?" he asked. He looked and looked.

Mia sat next to him. She held up a shape. "Look, a triangle," she said. It had three sides. It had three corners. Ibrahim touched each corner with his finger. "One, two, three," he counted. "Sides one, two, three." A triangle had three of each. It stood on top of Mia's house. The roof did not fall.

Ibrahim drew a triangle. He put it on top of his square. Now the house had a square body, a triangle roof, a rectangle door, and a round circle window. He counted the corners of the triangle again. "One, two, three." Then he yelled, "Teacher, look! My house!"

The teacher came over. She smiled at the triangle roof. "That house stands so tall," she said. Mia gave Ibrahim a brown crayon. He drew a brown spoon next to the door. "Who lives here?" Mia asked. "A cat," said Ibrahim. "A cat with three little kittens. One, two, three."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Hanging your coat on a hook keeps it off the floor.
story:
John was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma held out his red coat. "You can put it on yourself," she said. John pushed one arm in. He pushed the other arm in. The zipper was hard. He pulled it up, up, up. Click! It was closed all by himself.

"Time to go play," said Grandma. John wanted to take his coat off fast. He pulled and wiggled. Off it came. He dropped it on the floor. Then he ran to the kitchen for a snack.

Later, they heard a loud sound at the door. Grandpa came in with a big box. "Is John here?" he called. John ran to hug him. But first Grandma looked for his coat. Where was it? It was not on the chair. It was hiding on the floor! Grandpa stepped on something soft. "Oh no," he laughed. "A red frog!" It was just the coat.

The next day, John took off his coat again. He looked at the floor. He remembered Grandpa's big feet. So he reached up and hung his coat on the little hook by the door. The coat stayed up high, off the floor.

"There you are, red frog," John said, pointing up at the hook. Grandma laughed. "Nice work," she said. "Now let's go find a real frog in the garden."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: On a tablet, you tap the screen with your finger to choose things.
story:
Lena wanted to draw a yellow sun. Her teacher, Ms. Jo, held up the tablet. "I will turn it on," said Ms. Jo. She pushed the little button. The screen lit up.

Lena pressed her whole hand on the screen. She pressed hard. Nothing happened. The sun picture did not open. Lena frowned and tried again. Still nothing.

Ms. Jo knelt down beside her. "Try one finger," she said. "Tap, tap." Lena held out one finger. She tapped the screen, soft and light. Tap. The picture of a paint brush opened. Lena tapped again. Tap. The drawing app came up. There was the yellow color, right at the top. Lena tapped it and drew a big round sun.

Tommy came over. He could not open the app either. He pressed his whole hand on the screen. "Use one finger," Lena said. "Like this." She tapped the screen. Tap. The app opened for Tommy too. Lena drew one more sun. Then she put the tablet on the shelf, just where it belonged. "All done," she said. "Yellow sun for you, Ms. Jo."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours.
story:
Paint day was here. Charlotte wanted to paint a rainbow. She opened the paint box. There were only three pots. Red, yellow, and blue. "Where are all the colours?" she asked. Miss Pam smiled. "These are called the primary colours," she said. Charlotte frowned. "How can I paint a rainbow?" she asked. "Maybe I can find out," she said.

She dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. Swish, swish, on the paper. The colour turned orange! Charlotte gasped. Red and blue made purple. Yellow and blue made green. Her rainbow grew, stripe by stripe.

A boy named Leo leaned over. "How did you do that?" he asked. "The paints made new colours," Charlotte said. Outside, a dog began to bark at the sunny window. Charlotte painted one more orange stripe and held her rainbow up to the light.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Tomorrow is the day after today.
story:
Jasper stood by his window in his bedroom. He wanted to see Ben today. "Can we go to Ben's house now?" he asked. Mama shook her head. "Not today," she said. "Today we stay home. Tomorrow we go." Jasper frowned. He was sorry about waiting.

"Where is tomorrow?" he asked. Mama pointed at his bed. "Tomorrow comes after you sleep," she said. "Sleep now, and when you wake up, it will be tomorrow." Jasper looked at his bed. He looked at his window. He counted his toy cars. One, two, three. Then he put them away.

Jasper got into bed. Mama tucked him in. The room got dark and quiet. Jasper closed his eyes.

He woke up. Sun was on his blanket. "It is tomorrow!" he said. Mama smiled. "Yes. Now we can go." Jasper hugged his three cars. One, two, three. Then he ran to find his shoes.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street.
story:
Iris stood on her stool in the bathroom. She brushed her teeth by herself. The tap was shiny and silver. She wanted to wash her hands. She turned the tap a tiny bit. Warm water came out. Then Dad came in. "Let me check the hot side," he said. He felt the water with his hand. "Too hot. I will mix it for you." Dad turned the knobs. Now the water felt just right. Iris washed her hands in the nice warm water.

Then Iris looked out the little window. She could see the swings. The park was across the street. "Dad! The swings!" she said. Iris ran to the door. Dad took her hand at the curb. They waited together. Iris held Dad's hand tight while they crossed the street. Then she let go and ran to the swings.

On the way home, Iris stopped at the curb again. She put up her hand and said, "Hold my hand, Dad." Dad smiled and took it.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Wheels are round like circles, which lets them roll.
story:
Gabriel wanted to make a toy car. He found a small box. It looked like a rectangle. He found some cardboard and some tape. He cut four little squares. Squares for wheels!

Gabriel taped the square wheels on. He pushed the car. It went bump, bump, bump. It made a loud sound. "Silly car," said Gabriel. "Why won't you roll?"

Dad came to help. Dad cut four round wheels. "Circles," said Gabriel. He taped the circle wheels on. He pushed the car. It rolled fast across the floor! Gabriel ran to catch it. He picked it up with both hands and hugged it. "Round wheels win!" he shouted. Then he rolled the car right under Dad's arm. "Catch it, Dad!" called Gabriel.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
story:
Amira ran to the dress-up corner at school. Her tummy felt jumpy and excited. Today she would wear the red cape. But then she saw Ben. Ben sat under the table. Tears ran down his cheeks. He was crying.

Amira felt scared to go close. She took one little step. Then one more. "Why are you crying?" she asked. Ben sniffed. "My rabbit is gone," he said. His voice was sad. Amira thought and thought. When she felt sad, her bunny helped. So she got her bunny from her cubby. "You can hold her," she said.

Ben hugged the bunny. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile. "Thank you," he said. Amira smiled too. She felt happy inside. Later they built a nest of blocks for two toy birds. The red cape looked great on Ben. "Friends help friends," said Amira. Ben nodded and clapped.
